before: It flattered him. After being snubbed, he found it soothing that Mrs. Ramsay should confide this to him. Charles Tansley perked up. She suggested, too, how great a man’s intellect was, even as it declined, and how every wife was subordinate to her husband’s work—not that she blamed the girl, and the marriage had been happy enough, she believed—and this made him more pleased with himself than he had been so far. He would have liked, say, if they had taken a cab, to be the one to pay. And her little bag—might he carry it? No, no, she said, she always carried _that_ herself. And she did, too. Yes, he could sense that about her. He sensed a great many things, one thing especially that excited and unsettled him for reasons he could not put into words. He wanted her to see him in academic cap and gown, walking in a procession. A fellowship, a professorship—he felt he could do anything, and pictured himself—but what was she looking at? A man pasting up a poster. The enormous flapping sheet smoothed itself flat, and every sweep of the brush uncovered more legs, hoops, horses, gleaming reds and blues, beautifully sleek, until half the wall was taken up by a circus advertisement: a hundred horsemen, twenty performing seals, lions, tigers. … Leaning forward, because she was shortsighted, she read aloud that it … “will visit this town.” What terribly dangerous work, she exclaimed, for a man with one arm to stand at the top of a ladder like that—he had lost his left arm in a reaping machine two years ago.

before: There he stood in the front room of the cramped little house she had brought him to, waiting while she ran upstairs for a moment to see a woman. Above him he heard her quick step; heard her voice, bright, then quiet; looked at the mats, the tea caddies, the glass domes; waited with real impatience; looked eagerly ahead to the walk home, set on carrying her bag. Then he heard her come out; close a door; tell someone to keep the windows open and the doors shut, and to ask at the house for whatever they needed (she must be speaking to a child). And then, all of a sudden, in she came and stood silent for a moment (as though she had been playing a part up there, and now for a moment let herself simply be), stood perfectly still for a moment against a picture of Queen Victoria wearing the blue ribbon of the Garter; and all at once it came to him that it was this: it was this:—she was the most beautiful person he had ever seen.

before: Indeed, he nearly knocked her easel over, bearing down on her with his hands waving and shouting out “Boldly we rode and well.” But mercifully he turned sharply and rode off, to die gloriously, she supposed, on the heights of Balaclava, like Tennyson’s Light Brigade. Never was anybody at once so ridiculous and so alarming. But as long as he kept on like that, waving and shouting, she was safe; he would not stand still and look at her picture. And that was what Lily Briscoe could not have endured. Even while she looked at the mass, at the line, at the color, at Mrs. Ramsay sitting in the window with James, she kept a feeler out on her surroundings, in case someone should creep up and she should suddenly find her picture being looked at. But now, with all her senses sharpened as they were, looking and straining until the color of the wall and the clematis beyond burned into her eyes, she became aware of someone coming out of the house and coming toward her. Somehow she guessed from the footstep that it was William Bankes. So although her brush quivered, she did not turn her canvas face down on the grass, as she would have done if it had been Mr. Tansley, Paul Rayley, Minta Doyle, or practically anybody else. She let it stand. William Bankes stood beside her.

before: Yes. That was it. He was done. He turned away from the view. And as he turned to walk back the other way, up the drive, Mr. Bankes noticed things that would never have struck him if those sandhills had not shown him the body of his friendship, laid up in peat with the red on its lips. There was Cam, for instance, the little girl, Ramsay’s youngest daughter, picking sweet alyssum on the bank. She was wild and fierce. The nursemaid told her to “give a flower to the gentleman,” and she would not. No! no! no! she would not! She clenched her fist. She stamped her foot. And about his friendship Mr. Bankes felt aged and saddened, and somehow put in the wrong by her. He must have dried up and shrunk.

before: He stood stock-still by the urn, the geranium spilling over its rim. After all, he asked himself, out of a thousand million men, how many ever get to Z? Surely the leader of a forlorn hope has the right to ask that, and to answer, without betraying the expedition following him, “One, perhaps.” One in a generation. Should he be blamed, then, for not being that one? so long as he has worked honestly, given everything in his power, until there is nothing left to give? And how long will his fame last? Even a dying hero may be forgiven for wondering, before he dies, how men will talk of him when he is gone. Perhaps his fame will last two thousand years. And what are two thousand years? (asked Mr. Ramsay ironically, staring at the hedge). What indeed, if you gaze down from a mountaintop across the long wastes of the ages? The very stone your boot kicks aside will outlast Shakespeare. His own small light would shine for a year or two, not very brightly, and would then be swallowed up in some larger light, and that in a larger one still. (He peered into the darkness, into the tangle of twigs.) So who could blame the leader of that forlorn party—which has, after all, climbed high enough to see the waste of the years and the stars perishing—if, before death stiffens his limbs so that he can no longer move, he lifts his numb fingers to his brow a little deliberately and squares his shoulders, so that the search party, when it comes, will find him dead at his post, a fine figure of a soldier? Mr. Ramsay squared his shoulders and stood very straight beside the urn.

before: As he walked away, every beat of this pulse seemed to enclose her and her husband together, and to give each of them the comfort that two different notes, one high and one low, seem to give each other when they are struck at once and blend. But as the resonance faded, and she went back to the Fairy Tale, Mrs. Ramsay felt not just tired in body (she always felt this afterward, never at the time); her physical tiredness was also tinged with some faintly unpleasant feeling that had a different source. Not that she knew exactly what it came from as she read aloud the story of the Fisherman’s Wife. Nor would she let herself put her discontent into words when she saw—at the turn of the page, when she paused and heard, dully, ominously, a wave fall—what its source was. It was this. She disliked feeling, even for a second, that she was finer than her husband; and, beyond that, she could not stand being less than entirely sure, when she spoke to him, that what she said was true. The universities and the people who wanted him, the lectures and the books, and how supremely important they all were—none of that did she doubt for a moment. What unsettled her was the relationship between them, and the way he came to her like that, in the open, where anyone could see. Because then people said he depended on her, when they must surely know that he was by far the more important of the two, and that what she gave the world was nothing next to what he gave it. But then there was the other thing too: that she could not tell him the truth. She was afraid, say, about the greenhouse roof and how much it would cost to repair, fifty pounds perhaps; and about his books, afraid he might guess what she half suspected, that his latest book was not quite his best (she had picked that up from William Bankes); and then there were the small everyday things she hid, and the children noticing, and the weight it put on them. All this took away from the whole joy, the pure joy, of the two notes sounding together, and made the sound die in her ear now with a dreary flatness.

before: He made no answer. He took opium. According to the children, it had stained his beard yellow. Perhaps it had. What was plain to her was that the poor man was unhappy, and that he came to them every year to escape; and still, every year, she felt the same thing: he did not trust her. She would say, “I’m going into town. Can I get you stamps, paper, tobacco?” and feel him flinch. He did not trust her. His wife was to blame. She remembered the wicked way his wife had treated him, which had turned her, Mrs. Ramsay, to steel and adamant right there in that horrid little room in St. John’s Wood, when she had watched with her own eyes as that hateful woman turned him out of the house. He was untidy; he spilled things on his coat; he had all the tedious habits of an old man with nothing in the world to do; and she turned him out of the room. In her hateful way she said, “Now, Mrs. Ramsay and I want to have a little talk together,” and Mrs. Ramsay could see, as clearly as if they were before her eyes, the endless miseries of his life. Had he enough money for tobacco? Did he have to ask his wife for it? Half a crown? Eighteen pence? Oh, she could not bear to think of the small humiliations that woman put him through. And always now (she could not guess why, unless it came from that woman somehow) he shrank away from her. He never confided in her. Yet what more could she have done? A sunny room had been set aside for him. The children were kind to him. Not once had she shown any sign that he was unwelcome. In fact she went out of her way to be friendly. Do you want stamps, do you want tobacco? Here’s a book you might enjoy, and so on. And after all—after all (at this point, without being aware of it, she drew herself up, and the sense of her own beauty, so seldom present to her, came to her now)—after all, she did not usually find it hard to make people like her. There was George Manning, for example; Mr. Wallace; famous men though they were, they would come to see her in the evening, quietly, and talk with her alone by her fire. She could not help knowing that she carried the torch of her beauty with her wherever she went; she carried it high into every room she walked into. And after all, however much she might veil it, and shrink from the monotonous bearing it forced on her, her beauty showed. She had been admired. She had been loved. She had walked into rooms where people sat mourning. Tears had been shed in front of her. Men, and women too, had set aside the multitude of things in their lives and allowed themselves, with her, the relief of simplicity. It wounded her that he should shrink from her. It hurt. And yet it was not a clean hurt, not a right one. That was what bothered her, coming as it did on top of her discontent with her husband: the feeling she had now—as Mr. Carmichael shuffled past, barely nodding in answer to her question, a book under his arm, in his yellow slippers—that she was under suspicion; that all this longing of hers to give, to help, was vanity. Was it for her own gratification that she wanted so instinctively to help, to give, so that people would say of her, “O Mrs. Ramsay! dear Mrs. Ramsay … Mrs. Ramsay, of course!” and need her, and send for her, and admire her? Wasn’t this what she secretly wanted? And so when Mr. Carmichael drew back from her, as he was doing at this very moment, slipping away to some corner where he did his acrostic puzzles endlessly, she felt not simply rebuffed in her instinct, but made aware of the pettiness of some part of herself, and of human relations—how flawed they are, how contemptible, how selfish, even at their best. Worn out and shabby, and presumably no longer (her cheeks were hollow, her hair was white) a sight to fill anyone’s eyes with joy, she had better give her mind to the story of the Fisherman and his Wife, and so calm that bundle of sensitiveness, her son James (none of her children was as sensitive as he was).

before: Mr. Bankes was waiting for her reply. She was on the point of saying something against Mrs. Ramsay—that she was frightening too, in her own way, overbearing, or something of the kind—when Mr. Bankes’s rapture made it quite unnecessary for her to say anything at all. And rapture was the word, given that he was over sixty, and so clean and so impersonal, and seemed to go about clothed in a white scientist’s coat. The way Lily saw him gazing at Mrs. Ramsay was a rapture that matched, she felt, the passions of dozens of young men (and perhaps Mrs. Ramsay had never inspired the passions of dozens of young men). This was love, she thought, as she made a show of shifting her canvas—love distilled and filtered, love that never tried to grasp what it loved. Like the love mathematicians have for their symbols, or poets for their phrases, it was meant to spread across the world and add to what humanity had gained. And so, indeed, it was. The world ought by all means to have shared in it, if only Mr. Bankes could have explained why that woman gave him such pleasure. Why did watching her read a fairy tale to her little boy affect him in precisely the way a solved scientific problem did? He rested, contemplating it, and felt what he felt when he had proved something absolute about how plants digest: that barbarism had been tamed, and the reign of chaos brought under control.

Following the line of Mr. Bankes’s gaze toward Mrs. Ramsay, she thought that no woman could worship another woman as he worshipped her; women could only shelter together in the shade he cast over them both. Following his beam, she added her own, different ray. Mrs. Ramsay, she thought, was without question the loveliest of people (bent over her book there); perhaps the best; but also unlike the perfect form you saw before you. Yet why unlike, and unlike in what way? she wondered, scraping off her palette all those heaps of blue and green, which looked to her now like lifeless lumps of earth—though she swore that tomorrow she would breathe life into them, make them move and flow and obey her. In what way was Mrs. Ramsay different? What was the spirit in her, the essence, so that if you came across a glove tucked into the corner of a sofa you would know from its twisted finger that it was hers, beyond any doubt? For speed she was like a bird; for directness, an arrow. She was headstrong; she was commanding (naturally, Lily reminded herself, I’m thinking of how she is with women, and I’m much younger, a nobody, living off the Brompton Road). She threw open bedroom windows. She shut doors. (In this way Lily tried to get the tune of Mrs. Ramsay started in her head.) She would turn up late at night, tapping lightly on your bedroom door, wrapped in an old fur coat (that was always the setting for her beauty—hurried, but just right), and act out once again whatever it happened to be: Charles Tansley losing his umbrella; Mr. Carmichael snuffling and sniffing; Mr. Bankes announcing, “the vegetable salts are lost.” She would shape it all skillfully, even give it a malicious twist. Then she would move across to the window, pretending she had to go—it was dawn, she could see the sun coming up—and half turn back, more intimate now, yet still always laughing, to insist that she must, Minta must, all of them must marry. Because in the whole world, whatever laurels might be thrown her way (but Mrs. Ramsay didn’t care a fig about her painting), or whatever triumphs she might win (Mrs. Ramsay had probably had her share of those)—and here she grew sad and dark and returned to her chair—one thing was beyond dispute: an unmarried woman (she took Lily’s hand lightly for a moment), an unmarried woman has missed the best of life. The house seemed full of sleeping children and of Mrs. Ramsay listening; of lamps turned low and steady breathing.

before: Oh, but, Lily would answer, she had her father; her home; even, if she had dared say so, her painting. Yet set against the other thing, all of it seemed so slight, so virginal. Still, as the night went on and white light slipped between the curtains, and now and then some bird even chirped in the garden, she would summon up a desperate courage and argue that the universal law did not apply to her; beg to be excused from it. She liked being alone; she liked being herself; she wasn’t made for that. And then she would have to face a solemn look from eyes of matchless depth, and meet Mrs. Ramsay’s simple conviction (she was like a child now) that her dear Lily, her little Brisk, was a fool. Then, she remembered, she had put her head in Mrs. Ramsay’s lap and laughed and laughed and laughed—laughed almost hysterically at the idea of Mrs. Ramsay ruling, with unshakable calm, over destinies she didn’t understand in the least. There she sat, simple and serious. Lily had her sense of her back now—this was the glove’s twisted finger. But what sanctuary had she broken into? At last Lily Briscoe had raised her eyes, and there was Mrs. Ramsay, with no idea at all what had made her laugh, still presiding, but with every trace of willfulness gone now. In its place was something clear, like the space the clouds finally uncover—that little patch of sky asleep beside the moon.

before: She turned the page. Only a few lines were left, so she would finish the story, even though bedtime had passed. It was getting late. She could tell from the light in the garden; and the flowers turning white and something gray in the leaves combined to wake a feeling of anxiety in her. At first she couldn’t think what it was about. Then it came to her: Paul and Minta and Andrew weren’t back. Once more she summoned up the little group on the terrace outside the hall door, standing there looking up at the sky. Andrew had taken his net and basket. That meant he meant to catch crabs and so on. That meant he would clamber out onto some rock and be cut off by the tide. Or, coming home in single file along one of those narrow paths above the cliff, one of them might slip. He would roll, and then crash. It was getting quite dark.

before: He turned and saw her. Ah! She was lovely—lovelier now than ever, he thought. Yet he couldn’t speak to her. He couldn’t interrupt her. Now that James had gone and she was at last alone, he badly wanted to talk to her. But no, he decided; he wouldn’t interrupt. In her beauty, in her sadness, she stood apart from him now. He would leave her alone; and he went by without a word, though it hurt him that she looked so far away, that he couldn’t reach her, that there was nothing he could do for her. And once more he would have gone by without speaking, if she hadn’t, at that very moment, freely given him what she knew he would never ask for: she called to him, lifted the green shawl off the picture frame, and went to him. For he wanted, she knew, to protect her.

before: Paul and Minta went on ahead together, and he comforted her, telling her how famous he was for finding things. When he was a small boy he had once found a gold watch. He’d get up at daybreak, and he was certain he’d find it. It seemed to him it would still be nearly dark, and he’d be alone on the beach, and somehow there would be a bit of danger in it. Still, he began assuring her he would definitely find it, and she said she wouldn’t hear of him getting up at dawn: it was gone: she knew it was: she’d had a feeling when she put it on that afternoon. And privately he made up his mind not to tell her, but to slip out of the house at dawn while everyone slept; and if he couldn’t find it he’d go to Edinburgh and buy her another, exactly like it but lovelier. He’d show what he could do. And as they came out on the hill and saw the town’s lights below, the lights springing out one by one seemed like the things that were going to happen to him—his marriage, his children, his house. And once more, as they came out onto the main road, shaded by tall bushes, he thought of how they would withdraw into solitude together and walk on and on, he always leading, she pressed close at his side (as she was now). As they turned at the crossroads he thought what a terrifying ordeal he had been through, and that he had to tell someone—Mrs. Ramsay, naturally, for it took his breath away to think what he had been and what he had done. Asking Minta to marry him had been far and away the worst moment of his life. He’d go straight to Mrs. Ramsay, because somehow he felt she was the one who had made him do it. She’d made him think he could do anything. No one else took him seriously. But she made him believe he could do whatever he liked. All day today he had felt her eyes on him, following him everywhere (though she never said a word), as if she were saying, “Yes, you can do it. I believe in you. I expect it of you.” She had made him feel all that, and the moment they were back (he searched for the lights of the house above the bay) he would go to her and say, “I’ve done it, Mrs. Ramsay; thanks to you.” And so, turning into the lane that led to the house, he could see lights moving about in the upstairs windows. So they must be terribly late. People were dressing for dinner. The whole house was lit, and after the dark, the lights made his eyes feel full, and walking up the drive he said to himself, childishly, Lights, lights, lights, and said it over again in a daze, Lights, lights, lights, as they came into the house, staring around him, his face quite stiff. But good heavens, he told himself, reaching for his tie, I mustn’t make a fool of myself.)

before: But she let them take their time over it. Rose especially she let pick up first this and then that, and hold the jewels against the black dress; for this little ceremony of choosing jewels, gone through every night, was what Rose loved best, she knew. Rose had some secret reason of her own for thinking it tremendously important to choose what her mother wore. What could the reason be? Mrs. Ramsay wondered, standing still while Rose did up the clasp of the necklace she had picked. Through her own past she could guess at some deep, buried, wholly wordless feeling that you had for your mother at Rose’s age. Like every feeling felt for yourself, Mrs. Ramsay thought, it made you sad. What you could give back was so inadequate; and what Rose felt was out of all proportion to anything she really was. And Rose would grow up; and Rose would suffer, she supposed, with such deep feelings. Now she said she was ready, and they would go down, and Jasper, being the gentleman, should give her his arm, and Rose, being the lady, should carry her handkerchief (she handed her the handkerchief), and what else? Oh yes, it might be cold: a shawl. Choose me a shawl, she said, because that would please Rose, who was bound to suffer so. “There,” she said, pausing at the window on the landing, “there they are again.” Joseph had landed on a different treetop. “Don’t you think they mind,” she asked Jasper, “having their wings broken?” Why did he want to shoot poor old Joseph and Mary? He shuffled a bit on the stairs and felt told off, though not seriously, for she didn’t understand the fun of shooting birds; that birds didn’t feel; and being his mother, she lived far away in another part of the world. Still, he rather liked her stories about Mary and Joseph. She made him laugh. But how did she know those were Mary and Joseph? Did she think the same birds came to the same trees every night? he asked. But at this point, all of a sudden, she stopped paying him the slightest attention, the way grown-ups always did. She was listening to a clatter in the hall.

before: “You must hate eating in this madhouse,” she said, slipping, as she always did when her mind was elsewhere, into her social manner. It is the same as when a meeting breaks into a clash of voices, and the chairman, to restore unity, proposes that everyone speak French. The French may be bad; it may lack the words for what the speaker actually thinks; all the same, speaking French imposes a certain order, a certain sameness. Mr. Bankes answered her in the same language—“No, not at all”—and Mr. Tansley, who knew nothing of that language, even in words of one syllable like these, immediately suspected it of being insincere. The Ramsays really did talk nonsense, he thought, and he seized on this new example gleefully, making a note that some day he would read aloud to a friend or two. There, among people who could speak their minds, he would give a sarcastic account of “staying with the Ramsays” and the nonsense they talked. Worth doing once, he would say, but never again. The women were so boring, he would say. Ramsay, of course, had done for himself by marrying a beautiful woman and having eight children. It would come out roughly like that. But right now, stuck in his chair with an empty seat next to him, none of it had come out at all. It was nothing but scraps and fragments. He felt terribly uncomfortable, physically uncomfortable, even. He wanted someone to give him a chance to make his mark. He wanted it so badly that he squirmed in his chair, looked at one person and then another, tried to cut into their talk, opened his mouth and closed it again. They were discussing the fishing industry. Why didn’t anybody ask what he thought? What did they know about the fishing industry?

before: There is a code of manners, she knew, and its seventh article (possibly) states that on occasions like this one it falls to the woman, whatever her own work may be, to come to the aid of the young man across from her, so that he can bring out and ease the thighbones and ribs of his vanity, his pressing need to assert himself. Just as it is their duty, she thought, with her old-maidish sense of fair play, to help us if, for instance, the Underground caught fire. In that case, she thought, I’d certainly expect Mr. Tansley to get me out. But what if, she wondered, neither of us did either? So she sat there, smiling.

before: Now eight candles stood in a row down the table. After their first dip the flames straightened, and they drew the whole long table into view, and in its center a yellow and purple dish of fruit. What had she done with it? Mrs. Ramsay wondered. For Rose’s arrangement—the grapes and pears, the horny shell lined with pink, the bananas—made her think of a trophy hauled up from the seabed, of a banquet of Neptune, of the cluster of grapes that hangs with its vine leaves over Bacchus’s shoulder (in some painting or other), among leopard skins and torches flaring and drooping, red and gold. … Lifted suddenly into the light like that, it seemed enormous and deep, like a world where you could pick up your walking stick and climb its hills, she thought, and walk down into its valleys. And to her delight (because for a moment it made them feel in tune) she saw that Augustus, too, was feasting his eyes on the same dish of fruit: diving in, snapping off a bloom here, a tassel there, and then, having feasted, going back to his hive. That was how he looked at things, not the way she did. But looking together brought them together.

before: As usual, Lily thought. At that exact moment there was always something that had to be done — something Mrs. Ramsay, for private reasons, had decided to do at once, even if, as now, everyone was standing around making jokes, unable to make up their minds whether to go to the smoking-room, the drawing-room or up to the attics. And then, in the middle of all the noise, you would see Mrs. Ramsay standing there with Minta’s arm in hers, suddenly recollect, “Yes, it’s time for that now,” and slip off at once, secretive, to do something by herself. The minute she left, things began to fall apart. People drifted, hesitated, went their separate ways. Mr. Bankes took Charles Tansley by the arm and headed for the terrace to finish the political argument they had started over dinner, and that shifted the whole balance of the evening, tipped its weight another way. Watching them go, and catching a word or two about Labour Party policy, Lily felt as though the two men had climbed up to the ship’s bridge to take their bearings; that was how the switch from poetry to politics struck her. So off they went, Mr. Bankes and Charles Tansley, while the rest stood and watched Mrs. Ramsay climbing the stairs alone in the lamplight. Where, Lily wondered, was she off to in such a hurry?

before: But it wasn’t a picture of them, she said. Or not in the sense he meant. There were other ways, too, of honoring them. With a shadow here and a light there, for instance. That was the form her tribute took, if, as she vaguely assumed, a picture had to be a tribute. You could reduce a mother and child to a shadow without disrespect. A light here called for a shadow there. He thought it over. He was interested. He approached it scientifically, and in complete good faith. The fact was, he explained, all his prejudices ran the other way. The biggest picture in his drawing-room, which painters had admired and priced higher than what he had paid for it, showed the cherry trees in blossom along the banks of the Kennet. He had spent his honeymoon on the Kennet, he said. Lily must come and see that picture, he said. But now—he turned, spectacles raised, to examine her canvas scientifically. The question was one of how masses relate, how lights relate to shadows, and he had honestly never thought about that before; so he would like it explained to him. What, then, did she mean to make of it? And he pointed at the scene before them. She looked. She couldn’t show him what she meant to make of it; without a brush in her hand she couldn’t even see it herself. Once again she took up her old painting stance, eyes dimmed, manner absent, subduing all her impressions as a woman to something far more general. Once again she fell under the power of that vision she had once seen clearly and now had to grope for among hedges and houses and mothers and children—her picture. The question, she remembered, was how to join this mass on the right to that one on the left. She might do it by carrying the line of the branch across, like so; or she might break the empty foreground with some object (James, perhaps), like so. That was the form her tribute took, if, as she vaguely assumed, a picture had to be a tribute. You could reduce a mother and child to a shadow without disrespect. A light here called for a shadow there. He thought it over. He was interested. He approached it scientifically, and in complete good faith. The fact was, he explained, all his prejudices ran the other way. The biggest picture in his drawing room, which painters had admired and priced higher than what he had paid for it, showed the cherry trees in blossom along the banks of the Kennet. He had spent his honeymoon on the Kennet, he said. Lily must come and see that picture, he said. But now—he turned, spectacles raised, to examine her canvas scientifically. The question was one of how masses relate, how lights relate to shadows, and he had honestly never thought about that before; so he would like it explained to him. What, then, did she mean to make of it? And he pointed at the scene before them. She looked. She couldn’t show him what she meant to make of it; without a brush in her hand she couldn’t even see it herself. Once again she took up her old painting stance, eyes dimmed, manner absent, subduing all her impressions as a woman to something far more general. Once again she fell under the power of that vision she had once seen clearly and now had to grope for among hedges and houses and mothers and children—her picture. The question, she remembered, was how to join this mass on the right to that one on the left. She might do it by carrying the line of the branch across, like so; or she might break the empty foreground with some object (James, perhaps), like so. But the danger was that doing so might break the unity of the whole. She stopped; she didn’t want to bore him; she lifted the canvas gently off the easel.

before: she read, and turned the page, and swung herself, zigzagging here and there, from line to line as if from branch to branch, from one red and white flower to the next, until she was roused by a small sound — her husband slapping his thighs. For a second their eyes met; but neither wanted to talk. There was nothing to say, and still something seemed to pass between them, from him to her. It was the life of the book, its power, its enormous humor, she knew, that made him slap his thighs. Don’t interrupt, he seemed to be telling her; don’t speak; just sit. And he read on. His lips twitched. It filled him up. It gave him strength. All the petty irritations and jabs of the evening went clean out of his head — how unbearably dull he found it to sit still while people went on eating and drinking forever, how snappish he had been with his wife, how thin-skinned, how he had minded when they skipped over his books as if they did not exist. But now, he felt, it didn’t matter a damn who got to Z (if thought ran like an alphabet from A to Z). Someone would get there — if not he, then another man. The strength and sanity of this writer, his feeling for plain and simple things, these fishermen, the poor crazed old creature in Mucklebackit’s cottage (all in Scott’s The Antiquary), made him feel so full of vigor, so freed of something, that he was stirred and triumphant and could not choke back his tears. Lifting the book slightly to hide his face, he let the tears fall, and shook his head from side to side, and lost himself entirely (apart from one or two thoughts about morality, and French novels versus English ones, and how Scott’s hands were tied, though his view was perhaps as true as the other one) — lost all his own worries and failures in poor Steenie’s drowning and Mucklebackit’s grief (that was Scott at his finest) and in the astonishing pleasure and energy it gave him.

before: And then what? She could feel that he was still looking at her, but that the look was different now. He wanted something — the thing she always found so hard to give him: he wanted her to say that she loved him. And that, no, she could not do. Talking came so much more easily to him than to her. He was able to say things — she never was. So of course it was always he who said them; and then, for some reason, he would suddenly resent it and reproach her. A heartless woman, he called her; she never once told him she loved him. But that wasn’t true — it wasn’t true. It was only that she never could put what she felt into words. Wasn’t there a crumb on his coat? Nothing she could do for him? She got up and stood at the window holding the reddish-brown stocking, partly to turn away from him and partly because now, with him watching, she did not mind looking at the Lighthouse. For she knew he had turned his head when she turned; he was watching her. She knew what he was thinking: You are more beautiful than ever. And she felt very beautiful. Won’t you tell me just this once that you love me? That was what he was thinking, because he was stirred — what with Minta, and his book, and the day coming to an end, and their quarrel about going to the Lighthouse. But she couldn’t; she couldn’t say it. Then, knowing he was watching her, instead of speaking she turned around, the stocking in her hands, and looked at him. And as she looked at him she began to smile, for although she had not said a word, he knew — of course he knew — that she loved him. He could not deny it. And smiling, she looked out of the window and said (thinking to herself, Nothing on earth can equal this happiness) —
